subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 12 periods = 480 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 8h 0min

section_titles: NIM Game — Strategic Addition
periods.activity_title: Playing NIM: Adding 1 or 2 to Reach Ten

tasks_in_class.description: Play the two-player NIM game: each player alternately chooses 1 or 2 to add to the running total; first to reach 10 wins. Play for a few rounds.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Can you win the game if (a)(b)(c), p.149
tasks_in_class.description: Can you win if: (a) opponent reached 6, (b) opponent reached 7, (c) opponent reached 8 and it is your turn? Who wins in each case?

time_bands.activity: Introduce NIM Game, p.149 ("Play the two-player NIM game: each player alternately chooses 1 or 2....") — Pairs play three or four rounds. The teacher circulates, asking players to say each running total aloud so the class hears the addition accumulating.

Continue NIM Game, p.149 — After open play, guide children to ask: which running totals feel safe to land on? Introduce the idea of a 'safe number' — a total from which any opponent move leaves you in control.

Can you win the game if (a)(b)(c), p.149 ("Can you win if: (a) opponent reached 6, (b) opponent reached 7....") — Pairs work through all three cases and share conclusions. The class discusses what pattern links the safe numbers.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for children who add randomly and never ask why certain numbers feel winning — push them to articulate: 'If I land here, what can my opponent do?' A common error is thinking 9 is a safe number; help the class see that from 9 the opponent must reach exactly 10 in one move of 1.
materials: Chalkboard or whiteboard for recording running totals
Pencil and paper for each pair

section_titles: NIM Game — Strategic Addition
Addition Chart — Patterns in a Table
periods.activity_title: NIM Extended, Then Patterns in the Addition Table

tasks_in_class.description: Play the game with target numbers 10, 11, or 12. Find a number in each case at which you are sure you can win.
Identify some patterns in the addition table.
Observe where the number 9 appears in the table. How many times? What about other numbers?

time_bands.activity: NIM Game extension, p.150 ("Play the game with target numbers 10, 11, or 12....") — Pairs test each target. After play, groups share the safe number they found and the class compares across the three targets, looking for a rule.

Let Us Do Q1, p.150 ("Identify some patterns in the addition table.") — Students examine the printed 13×13 addition chart. Elicit observations: diagonal pattern, symmetry about the diagonal, how each row or column changes.

Let Us Do Q2, p.150 ("Observe where the number 9 appears in the table. How many times?....") — Students count occurrences of 9 and then choose another number. Class compares counts and reasons about why a number near the middle appears more often.

periods.teacher_notes: The backward-reasoning strategy built while working with strategic addition in NIM transfers naturally into reading the addition table: both involve asking 'what must have come before this total?' Encourage students to express the diagonal pattern in their own words before introducing formal vocabulary.

section_titles: Addition Chart — Patterns in a Table
periods.activity_title: Window Frames: Row, Column, and Diagonal Sums

tasks_in_class.description: Are there any rows or columns containing only even or only odd numbers? Explain your observation.
Red window frame: find row sums, column sums, diagonal sums; move frame to other places and compare. What do you notice?
Identify patterns and relationships among numbers in the blue window frame.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q3, p.150 ("Are there any rows or columns containing only even or only odd numbers?....") — Students scan the chart and record their finding. Class shares: odd-row + odd-row = even cell; mixed rows alternate. Encourage a verbal rule.

Let Us Do Q4(a)(b)(c)(d), p.151 ("Red window frame: find row sums, column sums, diagonal sums....") — Students place a 2×2 frame at one position, compute the four sums, then slide it to two more positions. Pairs share their numbers; the class hunts for what stays the same.

Let Us Do Q5, p.151 ("Identify patterns and relationships among numbers in the blue window frame.") — Students examine the blue frame and articulate any new relationship they notice. A quick class share closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is confusing 'row sum' with 'sum of the two row entries' — be explicit that the four numbers in a 2×2 frame form the window and students sum them two ways (row-wise then column-wise) to compare. Encourage students to state the equal-sum property as a sentence before moving on.

section_titles: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
periods.activity_title: Reversing Digits: What Sums Do We Always Get?

tasks_in_class.description: Take a 2-digit number (e.g. 27), reverse its digits (72), add them (99). Repeat for different 2-digit numbers.
What sums can we get when we add a 2-digit number with its reverse?
List all numbers which when added to their reverse give: (i) 55, (ii) 88.
Can we get a 3-digit sum? What is the smallest 3-digit sum that we can get?

homework.description: Number sequence on trees counting by 50 (2540, 2590, …); fill in the missing values.

time_bands.activity: Reverse and Add (a), p.151 ("Take a 2-digit number (e.g. 27), reverse its digits (72), add them (99)....") — Each student picks three different 2-digit numbers, reverses and adds. Results are written on the board.

Reverse and Add (b), p.151 ("What sums can we get when we add a 2-digit number with its reverse?") — Class pools their results and lists all distinct sums that appear. Students notice these are all multiples of 11 and try to explain why using the tens and units.

Reverse and Add (c), p.151 ("List all numbers which when added to their reverse give: (i) 55, (ii) 88.") — Pairs list numbers systematically. Class checks by adding, and discusses how to be sure they have found all cases.

Reverse and Add (d), p.151 ("Can we get a 3-digit sum? What is the smallest 3-digit sum....") — Students reason about the largest possible 2-digit reverse-and-add pair (e.g. 91+19) and decide whether a 3-digit result is possible.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is choosing a palindrome (like 11 or 22) and getting a result that 'looks wrong' — draw out that a palindrome reversed is itself, so the sum is simply double the number and still a multiple of 11. Encourage students to use place value language: 'the tens digit and the units digit swap.'

section_titles: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping

tasks_in_class.description: Number sequence on arches counting by 1000 (354, 1354, …); fill in the missing values.
Number line with kangaroo: fill missing values at equal intervals between 7645 and beyond 7745.
Karnataka has 6049 elephants and Kerala has 3054. How many elephants in total? Estimate the answer first.

time_bands.activity: Fill in the blanks (b), p.151 ("Number sequence on arches counting by 1000 (354, 1354, …)....") — Students complete the arch sequence independently, then pairs verify by adding 1000 each step.

Fill in the blanks (c), p.151 ("Number line with kangaroo: fill missing values at equal intervals....") — Students identify the interval, fill the blanks, and read their completed number line aloud to a partner.

How Many Animals? Q1, p.152 ("Karnataka has 6049 elephants and Kerala has 3054. How many in total?....") — Students estimate first, then model the addition using tokens (or drawings of blocks) for 1000, 100, 10, 1. The teacher shows the column algorithm alongside, emphasising that regrouping 10 ones as 1 ten is a place-value exchange. Students complete the column addition.

periods.teacher_notes: The skip-count tasks consolidate reading large numbers on a number line; this supports the estimation step that opens every wildlife problem. A very common error in the column addition is forgetting to write the regrouped digit above the next column — model placing it explicitly before computing that column.
materials: Place-value tokens or drawn Dienes block representations (1000, 100, 10, 1)

section_titles: How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping
periods.activity_title: Three-Addend Addition and Multi-Step Tiger Problems

tasks_in_class.description: Gujarat 1355, Karnataka 1131, Madhya Pradesh 1817 leopards. How many total? Estimate first.
Maharashtra has 444 tigers; MP has 341 more, Uttarakhand has 116 more. Find: (a) MP tigers, (b) UK tigers, (c) MP+UK total, (d) all three states total.

time_bands.activity: How Many Animals? Q2, p.153 ("Gujarat 1355, Karnataka 1131, Madhya Pradesh 1817 leopards. How many total?....") — Students estimate by rounding each number to the nearest hundred, then set up a 3-addend column. The teacher models adding the ones column first, carrying into tens, and so on.

How Many Animals? Q3(a)(b)(c)(d), p.154 ("Maharashtra has 444 tigers; MP has 341 more, Uttarakhand has 116 more....") — Students work parts (a) and (b) individually, then form small groups for (c) and (d), building a chain: each answer feeds the next question. Groups share and the class checks whether all chains land on the same grand total.

periods.teacher_notes: The chain structure of the tiger problem — each sub-answer feeding the next — is the unit's main teaching point; watch for children who re-read the original data at each step rather than using their computed answers. A common error is adding 341 and 116 both onto Maharashtra (444) rather than adding 116 onto the MP total.
materials: Place-value tokens or drawn block representations

section_titles: More or Less? — 4-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping

tasks_in_class.description: Assam has 5719 elephants, 3965 more than Meghalaya. How many elephants are in Meghalaya? Estimate first.
2022 leopard count in Central India and Eastern Ghats is 8820, up 749 from 2018. How many leopards were there in 2018? Estimate first.
Write the number of animals on the India map using data from previous problems (elephants, tigers, leopards by state/region).

time_bands.activity: More or Less? Q1, p.155 ("Assam has 5719 elephants, 3965 more than Meghalaya. How many in Meghalaya?....") — Students estimate first, then model regrouping: 1 hundred = 10 tens, 1 thousand = 10 hundreds, using tokens or drawings. The teacher shows the column subtraction alongside, naming each regrouping step.

More or Less? Q2, p.155–156 ("2022 leopard count is 8820, up 749 from 2018. How many in 2018?....") — Students work independently, estimating first. The teacher circulates, checking that students subtract 749 from 8820 (not the reverse). Pairs compare and reconcile.

Map activity, p.156 ("Write the number of animals on the India map....") — Students locate each state on the printed map outline and write in the animal count derived from prior calculations. This situates the numbers in a real geographic context.

periods.teacher_notes: The regrouping sequence mirrors the addition work done with elephant and leopard counts: 10 ones become 1 ten in addition becomes 1 ten back into 10 ones in subtraction — name this connection explicitly. A common error is subtracting the larger digit from the smaller without regrouping; encourage students to check by adding their answer back to the smaller number.
materials: Place-value tokens or drawn Dienes block representations
Printed India map outline per student

section_titles: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
periods.activity_title: Kaziranga Visitors and Juice Factory: Multi-Step Problems

tasks_in_class.description: Kaziranga: Dec 8591, Nov 6415 visitors. (a) How many more in Dec than Nov? (b) Nov is 1587 more than Oct; find Oct visitors.
Juice factory: pineapple 1348, passion fruit 4781. (a) Guava = pineapple + 759. (b) Orange = guava + 1257. (c) Is guava + orange more or less than passion fruit?

homework.description: Vehicles: jeeps 6304. (a) Buses = jeeps + 253. (b) Tractors = buses − 5247. (c) Taxis = tractors + 1579. (d) Arrange vehicle counts lowest to highest.

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q1(a)(b), p.157 ("Kaziranga: Dec 8591, Nov 6415 visitors. (a) How many more in Dec....") — Students identify which operation each part needs before computing. Part (b) requires subtraction; check that students recognise 'Nov is 1587 more than Oct' means Oct = Nov − 1587.

Let Us Do Q2(a)(b)(c), p.157–158 ("Juice factory: pineapple 1348, passion fruit 4781. (a) Guava = pineapple + 759....") — Students solve in a chain: guava first, then orange using guava, then the comparison. Groups share and debate (c): is the comparison answerable without exact computation?

periods.teacher_notes: The juice factory problem is another chain, like the tiger problem from the wildlife census section — each intermediate answer feeds the next. Watch for students who restart with given data for each part rather than carrying forward their computed values. For part (c), encourage estimation before exact addition.

section_titles: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
periods.activity_title: Column Drill and Baal Mela Deposit Slips

tasks_in_class.description: Solve 10 addition and subtraction problems: e.g. 1459+476, 3863+4188, 7293−2819, 8006−5567 (4-digit).
Baal Mela: help Raju (₹2045), Rani (₹3578), Roja (₹1240) fill deposit slips with possible combinations of notes (500, 100, 50, 10) and coins (5, 2, 1).

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q4(a)–(j), p.158 ("Solve 10 addition and subtraction problems: e.g. 1459+476, 3863+4188....") — Students work individually on all ten problems in column form. After an unhurried working period, pairs swap and check each other's carrying and borrowing digits.

Let Us Do Q5, p.159–160 ("Baal Mela: help Raju ₹2045, Rani ₹3578, Roja ₹1240 fill deposit slips....") — The teacher introduces the deposit slip format and discusses denominations. Small groups each tackle one person's amount, finding at least two different valid combinations. Groups share strategies; the class notices how place value knowledge (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) guides denomination choices.

periods.teacher_notes: The deposit slip task is an open decomposition puzzle — multiple valid answers exist, so students should be encouraged to find more than one and explain why each works. A common error is using too many of one denomination; ask 'Can you use fewer notes of that value and replace them with smaller ones?'
materials: Sample deposit slip drawn on the board
Optional: play notes and coins if available

section_titles: Let Us Solve — Column Algorithm Practice
periods.activity_title: Column Form Consolidation: Four Pre-Set and Eight Notebook Problems

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q1(a)(b)(c)(d), p.161 ("Solve 4 column-format problems: (a) 3695+4208, (b) 2507+6847....") — Students complete all four problems in the pre-formatted columns. The teacher checks for correct regrouping notation — small carried digits written above the column — before moving on.

Let Us Solve Q2(a)–(h), p.161 ("Arrange in columns and solve in notebook: 3683−971, 8432−46....") — Students set up their own columns in notebooks for all eight expressions. Emphasis is on aligning digits correctly when one number has fewer digits (e.g. 8432−46). Partners exchange notebooks and verify two problems each.

periods.teacher_notes: Column alignment when the numbers have different digit counts (e.g. 8432−46) is the main pitfall here — model placing 46 so its units digit sits under the units column of 8432, not under the tens. Encourage students to draw faint place-value column lines if alignment is uncertain.

section_titles: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
periods.activity_title: Easy Ways, Comparisons, and Derived Facts in Addition and Subtraction

tasks_in_class.description: Find easy ways to solve 9 problems (e.g. 8787−99, 4596+104, 3999+290). Share thinking with the class.
Use <, =, > to compare 4 expression pairs without calculating (e.g. 54+97 vs 54+90; 73−54 vs 73−56). Reason and share.
Fill a 3×3 grid with numbers 1–9 so the difference between any two neighbouring squares (connected by a line) is odd. Find other ways. Can you make all differences even?

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q1(a)–(i), p.162 ("Find easy ways to solve 9 problems (e.g. 8787−99, 4596+104)....") — Students attempt each problem mentally or with minimal writing, then share strategies. Record 'subtract 100, add 1' and similar rules on the board.

Let Us Solve Q2, p.162 ("Use <, =, > to compare 4 expression pairs without calculating....") — Students reason aloud: 'Both have 54 added; 97 > 90, so the left side is larger.' The teacher encourages verbal justification before any digit is written.

Let Us Solve Q3, p.162 ("Use given equations to find derived values: e.g. 139+175=314 → 314−175=?....") — Students identify the relationship between the given fact and the derived one (inverse, one more, compensation) and write the answer without full computation.

Fill the squares Q3, p.163 ("Fill a 3×3 grid with numbers 1–9 so the difference between any two neighbouring squares is odd....") — Groups place digits and test neighbours; the class discusses whether an all-even-difference version is possible and why.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error in the derived-fact problems is re-computing from scratch instead of adjusting — push students to say 'I need to change only one addend by 1, so the sum changes by 1.' The grid puzzle connects parity reasoning (odd ± even = odd) to subtraction, which ties the two threads of this section together.
materials: Grid template drawn on paper or board for the squares puzzle

periods.activity_title: From NIM to Number Sense: A Whole-Chapter Celebration

time_bands.activity: Strategy revisit — the class plays one rapid round of NIM (target 10) and then one round with a target of 11 or 12, naming aloud the 'safe numbers' they recall from strategic-addition reasoning. The quick game warms up mental arithmetic and connects counting-by-small-steps to number sense.

Pattern gallery — small groups each take one question: (a) What do all reverse-and-add results have in common? (b) In a 2×2 window on the addition chart, which sums are always equal? (c) If you add a 2-digit number and its reverse, can you ever get a 3-digit answer? Groups prepare a two-sentence answer and share it with the class, building a collective summary of the structural patterns discovered across the chapter.

Wildlife calculation relay — the teacher reads two or three fresh animal-census-style problems combining 4-digit addition and subtraction with regrouping (numbers different from any textbook task). Students estimate first, then solve in column form, connecting the regrouping rules from the elephants, leopards, and tiger sections. One student per group explains the regrouping step used.

Mental strategy share — each student writes one 'easy way' they now use for addition or subtraction (e.g. rounding to a near-hundred, using a known fact to derive a new one, comparing without computing). Partners read each other's strategy and decide whether it always works or only sometimes, closing the unit with a moment of critical reflection on the mental arithmetic methods built through the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together every strand of the chapter: game-based strategic thinking from NIM, structural patterns from the addition chart and reverse-and-add exploration, column algorithm fluency from the wildlife and word problem sections, and flexible mental strategies. Where students give incomplete strategy explanations in the final band, ask 'Does this always work? Can you show a case where it might not?'
materials: Optional: printed India map for reference during the relay

items.prompt: Priya and Dev are playing NIM. They take turns adding 1 or 2 to a running total. The first player to reach 10 wins. The total is now 7 and it is Priya's turn. What should Priya add to be sure she wins?

options.label: D
options.text: Either 1 or 2 — Priya wins whichever she picks

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Either 1 or 2 — Priya wins whichever she picks. If she adds 1 (total 8), Dev can add only 1 or 2, giving 9 or 10; Priya then completes to 10. If she adds 2 (total 9), Dev can add only 1, giving 10 — wait, that means Dev reaches 10 and wins. So the correct winning move is to add 1, reaching 8, leaving Dev in a losing position. Rechecking: from 8, Dev adds 1 → 9, Priya adds 1 → 10 (Priya wins); Dev adds 2 → 10 (Dev wins). From 8, Dev can reach 10, so 8 is not fully safe. Actually from 7: add 3 is not allowed. Add 1 → 8 (Dev can add 2 → 10, Dev wins). Add 2 → 9 (Dev adds 1 → 10, Dev wins). So from 7, whichever Priya adds, Dev wins on the next move.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Work backwards from 10: the player who faces a total of 7 cannot prevent the opponent from reaching 10 in one move.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks landing on 8 guarantees a win, not recognising Dev can add 2 to reach 10 immediately.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student thinks landing on 9 is safe, not recognising Dev can add 1 to reach 10 immediately.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student thinks adding 3 is allowed, misreading the rule that only 1 or 2 may be added per turn.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student act out the moves with counters on a number strip; stretch: ask what total below 7 would have given Priya a guaranteed win.

exercise.description: Play the two-player NIM game: each player alternately chooses 1 or 2 to add to the running total; first to reach 10 wins. Play for a few rounds.

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: Meena takes the number 36, reverses its digits to get 63, and adds them: 36 + 63. Ravi takes the number 45, reverses its digits to get 54, and adds them: 45 + 54. Without calculating, what do you think is true about both their answers? Write one sentence.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: When a 2-digit number is added to its digit-reversal, the tens and units digits swap roles, so the sum always equals 11 times the sum of the two digits.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to compute both sums and look at what number divides both exactly; stretch: ask whether 62 + 26 and 53 + 35 give the same result as 36 + 63, and why.

exercise.description: Take a 2-digit number (e.g. 27), reverse its digits (72), add them (99). Repeat for different 2-digit numbers.

items.prompt: In NIM the target is 10. The running total is 6 and it is your turn. Your friend says: 'Whatever you add, I will win.' Is your friend right? Explain your thinking in one or two sentences.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, the friend is right. If you add 1 (total 7), the friend adds 2 (total 9), and then whatever you add (1 or 2) the friend can reach 10. If you add 2 (total 8), the friend adds 2 (total 10) and wins immediately. Either way the friend wins.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Work backwards from 10: 7 and 8 both leave the next player able to force a win, so 6 is a losing position for the player whose turn it is.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically act out both possibilities with a number strip and counters; stretch: ask what the losing position would be if the target were 11 instead of 10.

exercise.book_ref: Can you win the game if (a)(b)(c), p.149
exercise.description: Can you win if: (a) opponent reached 6, (b) opponent reached 7, (c) opponent reached 8 and it is your turn? Who wins in each case?

items.prompt: When playing NIM with a target of 12, which running total, if you land on it, guarantees that you can win no matter what your opponent does next?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9. From 9, the opponent must add 1 or 2. If the opponent adds 1 (total 10), you add 2 to reach 12 and win. If the opponent adds 2 (total 11), you add 1 to reach 12 and win. So 9 is the guaranteed winning position.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Work backwards from the target 12: the safe position is 12 − 3 = 9, because whatever the opponent adds (1 or 2), you can complete the total to 12.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student subtracts 2 from 12 rather than 3, finding only one safe gap instead of the full step of 3.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student subtracts 1 from 12, thinking only one opponent move needs to be covered.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student applies the target-10 safe position (7) shifted by 1 without re-reasoning for target 12.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student trace possible moves from each candidate total to see which always reaches 12; stretch: ask what the safe position would be if the target were 15.

exercise.description: Play the game with target numbers 10, 11, or 12. Find a number in each case at which you are sure you can win.

items.section_title: Addition Chart — Patterns in a Table
items.prompt: Look at any 2×2 window placed on the addition chart. Arun adds the two numbers in the top row and gets a sum. Bina adds the two numbers in the bottom row. What is always true about their two sums?

options.label: A
options.text: Arun's sum and Bina's sum are always equal.

options.label: B
options.text: Arun's sum is always larger than Bina's sum.

options.label: C
options.text: Bina's sum is always exactly 1 more than Arun's sum.

options.label: D
options.text: The two sums are sometimes equal and sometimes different.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Arun's sum and Bina's sum are always equal. In any 2×2 window the row sums equal each other (and equal the column sums and diagonal sums), because the four numbers form a pattern in which opposite pairs compensate.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: In a 2×2 window on the addition chart, moving one step right increases by 1 and moving one step down increases by 1, so both row sums and both column sums equal the same total.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student assumes the top row always has smaller addends without checking the structure of the chart.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student notices that numbers increase by 1 across columns but incorrectly applies this to the sums rather than the individual entries.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not tested enough window positions to see the invariant relationship.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a specific 2×2 window and ask them to compute both row sums before answering; stretch: ask whether the diagonal sums in the same window are also equal to the row sums, and why.

exercise.description: Red window frame: find row sums, column sums, diagonal sums; move frame to other places and compare. What do you notice?

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: A 2-digit number is added to its digit-reversal and the answer is 55. Write all the 2-digit numbers for which this is true.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The pairs are: 14 and 41, 23 and 32. (14+41=55; 23+32=55. Also note that a number and its reversal are both counted, so the list is: 14, 41, 23, 32.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The sum of a 2-digit number and its reversal equals 11 times the sum of the two digits; set 11×(digit sum) = 55 to find digit sum = 5, then list all 2-digit pairs with digits summing to 5.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to list all pairs of digits that add to 5 (1+4, 2+3) and form numbers from each pair; stretch: ask them to list all numbers whose reverse-and-add gives 77.

exercise.description: List all numbers which when added to their reverse give: (i) 55, (ii) 88.

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: When you add a 2-digit number to its digit-reversal, can the answer ever be a 3-digit number? Choose the correct statement.

options.label: A
options.text: No; adding two 2-digit numbers always gives a 2-digit answer.

options.label: B
options.text: No; the largest reverse-and-add sum for 2-digit numbers is 99.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes; the largest possible sum is 99 + 99 = 198, but 99 is a palindrome so this does not count as a reversal — the largest genuine sum is 91 + 19 = 110, which is 3 digits.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes; the largest genuine (non-palindrome) reverse-and-add sum is 91 + 19 = 110, which is a 3-digit number.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Try the 2-digit number with the largest possible digit sum where the two digits differ: 91 + 19 = 110.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student uses a palindrome (99 reversed is 99) which does not give a true reversal pair, showing they have not checked the palindrome condition.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student overgeneralises: two 2-digit numbers can sum above 99 (e.g. 91+19=110), so the claim is false.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student takes 99 as the maximum without testing near-maximum non-palindrome pairs such as 91+19.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to compute 91+19 and decide whether 110 has three digits; stretch: ask what the second-largest 3-digit reverse-and-add sum is.

exercise.description: Can we get a 3-digit sum? What is the smallest 3-digit sum that we can get?

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
items.prompt: A school collected ₹2050 for a fundraiser. The teacher wants to deposit this using only ₹500 notes, ₹100 notes, and ₹50 notes. Write one way to make exactly ₹2050 using these denominations. How many notes of each kind did you use?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid answer: four ₹500 notes (₹2000) + one ₹50 note (₹50) = ₹2050. Another valid answer: three ₹500 notes (₹1500) + five ₹100 notes (₹500) + one ₹50 note (₹50) = ₹2050. Any correct combination is accepted.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Break the amount by place value: 2050 = 2000 + 50; cover 2000 with ₹500 or ₹100 notes and 50 with a ₹50 note.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a place-value table (Th H T O) and ask which denomination covers each column; stretch: find a second way to make ₹2050 using a different combination and explain the difference.

exercise.description: Baal Mela: help Raju (₹2045), Rani (₹3578), Roja (₹1240) fill deposit slips with possible combinations of notes (500, 100, 50, 10) and coins (5, 2, 1).

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
items.prompt: Solve 5200 − 99 without using the column method. Write the answer and explain your shortcut in one sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5200 − 99 = 5101. Shortcut: subtract 100 to get 5100, then add 1 back to get 5101.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Treat 99 as 100 − 1: subtract 100 from 5200 to get 5100, then compensate by adding 1.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: first ask the student to compute 5200 − 100 and then ask what must be added back; stretch: use the same strategy to compute 6300 − 199 and explain why it works.

exercise.description: Find easy ways to solve 9 problems (e.g. 8787−99, 4596+104, 3999+290). Share thinking with the class.

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
items.prompt: You know that 248 + 135 = 383. Without calculating again, what is 248 + 136?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 384. Since 136 is one more than 135, and 248 stays the same, the sum is one more than 383.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: When one addend increases by 1 and the other stays the same, the sum also increases by 1.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student subtracted 1 from the known sum instead of adding 1, confusing the direction of change.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student copied the known sum without adjusting for the changed addend.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 2 instead of 1, perhaps thinking both addends changed.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 248+135=383 and circle only the digit that changed (5→6), then ask by how much the answer must change; stretch: ask what 247+136 equals, requiring adjustment in a different addend.

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Mental Strategies and Reasoning
items.prompt: In the 3×3 grid puzzle, you must place numbers so that the difference between every pair of neighbouring squares is odd. Raju placed an odd number in one square and an even number in the square next to it. Their difference is odd. Can two odd numbers or two even numbers be placed next to each other? Explain why or why not in one sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No. The difference of two odd numbers is even, and the difference of two even numbers is also even, so neighbours must always be one odd and one even to keep the difference odd.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the rule: odd − even = odd and even − odd = odd, whereas odd − odd = even and even − even = even.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to compute 3−1, 4−2, and 3−2, then classify each difference as odd or even; stretch: ask whether it is possible to colour the 3×3 grid like a chessboard (alternating odd and even) and fill it with 1–9 so that every neighbour pair has an odd difference.

exercise.description: Fill a 3×3 grid with numbers 1–9 so the difference between any two neighbouring squares (connected by a line) is odd. Find other ways. Can you make all differences even?

items.section_title: Reverse and Add — Digit Patterns and Sequences
items.prompt: A number line shows counts by equal jumps. The first two values are 6425 and 6450. What are the next two values on the number line?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6475 and 6500. The jump is 6450 − 6425 = 25, so each next value adds 25.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the interval by subtracting consecutive given values, then add the interval repeatedly.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student uses intervals of 20 then 20, perhaps adding only the tens digit each time.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student uses an interval of 50 instead of 25, possibly doubling the correct jump.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student uses an interval of 10 then 15, applying an inconsistent step.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to subtract 6425 from 6450 to find the jump before filling the blanks; stretch: ask what the eighth value on the number line would be.

exercise.description: Number line with kangaroo: fill missing values at equal intervals between 7645 and beyond 7745.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the column algorithm with regrouping: carry tens and hundreds in addition; borrow hundreds and thousands in subtraction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a blank column-form grid and ask the student to write digits in their correct place-value columns before adding or subtracting; stretch: ask the student to verify the subtraction answer by adding 3556 + 3456 and checking the result matches 7012.

exercise.description: Solve 10 addition and subtraction problems: e.g. 1459+476, 3863+4188, 7293−2819, 8006−5567 (4-digit).

items.section_title: Let Us Solve — Column Algorithm Practice

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Regroup across zeros: 9000 becomes 8999 + 1 in the ones place after successive borrowing through hundreds and tens.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the student how to regroup 9000 as 8 thousands + 9 hundreds + 9 tens + 10 ones step by step before subtracting; stretch: ask the student to check the answer by adding 4363 + 4637 and verifying the sum is 9000.

items.section_title: How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping
items.prompt: A forest reserve counted 2748 deer and 3865 peacocks. How many animals are there in total? Estimate the answer first, then find the exact total.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Estimate by rounding to the nearest hundred, then use the column algorithm with regrouping ones to tens and tens to hundreds.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to use place-value tokens (drawings of blocks for 1000, 100, 10, 1) to model the regrouping before writing the column sum; stretch: ask how many more animals the reserve needs to reach exactly 7000.

exercise.description: Karnataka has 6049 elephants and Kerala has 3054. How many elephants in total? Estimate the answer first.

items.section_title: How Many Animals? — 4-Digit Addition with Regrouping
items.prompt: A state A has 562 deer. State B has 215 more deer than State A. State C has 318 more deer than State B. (a) How many deer are in State B? (b) How many deer are in State C? (c) How many deer are in States B and C together?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Build a chain: compute B from A, then C from B, then add B and C, using the column algorithm with regrouping at each step.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw a chain diagram labelling A → B → C with the 'add' arrows before computing; stretch: ask for the total of all three states.

exercise.description: Maharashtra has 444 tigers; MP has 341 more, Uttarakhand has 116 more. Find: (a) MP tigers, (b) UK tigers, (c) MP+UK total, (d) all three states total.

items.section_title: More or Less? — 4-Digit Subtraction with Regrouping
items.prompt: A wildlife sanctuary in State X has 4312 birds. This is 1758 more than the number of birds in State Y. How many birds are in State Y? Estimate the answer first, then calculate.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise 'X has 1758 more than Y' means Y = X − 1758; apply column subtraction with regrouping tens, hundreds, and thousands.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to verify by checking that 2554 + 1758 = 4312; stretch: ask how many more birds Y would need to reach exactly 3000.

exercise.description: Assam has 5719 elephants, 3965 more than Meghalaya. How many elephants are in Meghalaya? Estimate first.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
items.prompt: A zoo counted 7240 visitors in March and 5863 visitors in February. (a) How many more visitors came in March than in February? (b) January had 1324 fewer visitors than February. How many visitors came in January?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 7240 − 5863 = 1377 more visitors in March. (b) 5863 − 1324 = 4539 visitors in January.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Part (a): subtract February from March; part (b): subtract 1324 from February's count, using the column algorithm with regrouping.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to underline the operation word in each part ('how many more' → subtract; 'fewer' → subtract) before computing; stretch: ask for the total visitors across all three months.

exercise.description: Kaziranga: Dec 8591, Nov 6415 visitors. (a) How many more in Dec than Nov? (b) Nov is 1587 more than Oct; find Oct visitors.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Word Problems and Money
items.prompt: A factory makes 2156 mango drinks. It makes 843 more guava drinks than mango drinks. It makes 1265 more orange drinks than guava drinks. (a) How many guava drinks does it make? (b) How many orange drinks does it make? (c) Are guava and orange drinks together more or less than 7000? By how much?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Build the chain using column addition; then add the two results and compare with 7000 by subtraction.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw boxes labelled Mango → Guava → Orange with arrows and fill in each count step by step; stretch: ask how many more orange drinks than mango drinks the factory makes.

exercise.description: Juice factory: pineapple 1348, passion fruit 4781. (a) Guava = pineapple + 759. (b) Orange = guava + 1257. (c) Is guava + orange more or less than passion fruit?
